name.text: Equations in sin squared and cos squared

questiontext.text:
Solve \({@p@}\sin^2 x = {@q@}\cos^2 x\) for \(0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ\). Give angles that are not whole numbers to 1 decimal place.

\(x \in\) [[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]

generalfeedback.text:
Divide both sides by \({@p@}\cos^2 x\). Since \(\dfrac{\sin x}{\cos x} = \tan x\),

\[\tan^2 x = {@k@}, \qquad \tan x = {@rk@} \text{ or } \tan x = -{@rk@}.\]

\(\tan x = {@rk@}\) gives \(x = {@degraw(al)@}\) (calculator) and \(180^\circ + {@degraw(al)@}\); \(\tan x = -{@rk@}\) gives \(180^\circ - {@degraw(al)@}\) and \(360^\circ - {@degraw(al)@}\), because tan repeats every \(180^\circ\).

So \(x \in {@setraw(sols)@}\).

No solution is lost by dividing: if \(\cos x = 0\) then \(\sin^2 x = 1\), and the left side is \({@p@}\), not \(0\).

questiondescription.text:
Trigonometry III: equations in sin squared and cos squared

Grade 12 CBE Core 2.5: Solve p sin^2 x = q cos^2 x for 0 to 360 degrees by dividing to obtain tan^2 x.

Core

This question is adapted from Example 11 in Section E of Chapter 7 of Cassell, D., Instone, S., Ling, J., Scruton, P., Shilton, S. and West, H., SMP AS/A2 Mathematics: Core 2 for AQA, Cambridge University Press, 2004: degrees instead of radians, new ratios, randomised over a curated list, with the answer typed as a set and named feedback for the usual errors.

INNODEMS CBC Grade 12 Mathematics, first draft by Ben Davies, 2026. Aligned to the KICD Senior School Curriculum Design, Core Mathematics Grade 12 (draft).

truefeedback.text: \(\tan^2 x = {@k@}\) gives \(\tan x = {@rk@}\) or \(\tan x = -{@rk@}\). You used only the positive root.
Dividing \({@p@}\sin^2 x = {@q@}\cos^2 x\) by \({@p@}\cos^2 x\) gives \(\tan^2 x = {@k@}\), not \({@1/k@}\).
Those solve \(\tan x = {@k@}\). Here \(\tan^2 x = {@k@}\): take the square root first.

Every angle you gave is a solution, but the equation has {@length(solsF)@} solutions in \(0^\circ \le x \le 360^\circ\) and you gave {@length(sl)@}.[[if test="miss360"]] When \(0^\circ\) is a solution, \(360^\circ\) is one too: both ends are in the interval.[[/if]]

[[if test="is(extras = [])"]]You have every solution, but you gave at least one of them twice, to different accuracy. Give each angle once.[[else]]You have every solution, but also {@setstr(extras)@}.[[/if]][[if test="is(outside # [])"]] Angles outside \(0^\circ\) to \(360^\circ\) are not wanted: add or subtract \(360^\circ\) to bring a calculator value into the interval.[[/if]]

Each of your angles is close to a solution, but not correct to 1 decimal place. Keep full calculator accuracy and round only at the end, to 1 decimal place (round up when the next digit is 5 or more).

Test your angles in the equation. For \({@p@}\sin^2 x - {@q@}\cos^2 x\), {@resstr@}. A solution gives \(0\).

[[/if]]

Divide both sides by \(\cos^2 x\) to get an equation in \(\tan^2 x\). Take both square roots and find two angles for each (tan repeats every \(180^\circ\)).

Angles outside \(0^\circ\) to \(360^\circ\) are not wanted: add or subtract \(360^\circ\) to bring a calculator value into the interval.

[[/if]][[if test="radn"]]

All your values are small: check that your calculator is in degree mode, and give angles in degrees.
